extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing §101 guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claims (especially computer-implemented/software claims) are 'directed to' an abstract idea under the §101 two-step framework (Step 2A/2B), using recent Federal Circuit decisions (Enfish; TLI) as instructive examples. Focuses on how to interpret claim focus, use the specification, and assess additional elements for 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare claim to previously found-abstract claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it is appropriate to compare the claim to claims already found to be directed to an abstract idea in a previous court decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior court decisions to identify whether the concept recited by the claim is similar to concepts previously held abstract. Examiners are to determine if the claim recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) a concept that is similar to concepts previously found abstract by the courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Directed to" inquiry considers claim as a whole in view of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'directed to' inquiry applies a filter to claims, when interpreted in view of the specification, based on whether their character as a whole is directed to a patent ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the claim in light of the specification to determine the focus of the claimed invention (its character as a whole), rather than isolating elements or ignoring specification teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid describing claims at a high level untethered from claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution against describing a claim at a high level of abstraction untethered from the language of the claim when determining the focus of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not abstractly summarize the claim into overly broad categories; instead, focus on what the claim actually recites and how the specification characterizes the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running on a general-purpose computer is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention's ability to run on a general purpose computer does not automatically doom the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere fact that software runs on conventional computer hardware does not make the claim directed to an abstract idea; evaluate whether the claim is directed to an improvement in computer-related technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to improvements in computer-related technology may be non-abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claims directed to improvements in computer-related technology, including claims directed to software, are not necessarily abstract (Step 2A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is directed to a specific improvement in computer functionality (analogous to chip architecture or an LED display), it can demonstrate the claim is not similar to previously identified abstract ideas and may be patent eligible at Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software can make non-abstract improvements like hardware can
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining that software can make non-abstract improvements to computer technology just as hardware can, the court noted that claims directed to software, as opposed to hardware, also are not inherently abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat software claims as presumptively abstract; assess whether the software claim recites a specific technical improvement to computer capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish focus: improvement in computer capabilities vs abstract process using computers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the focus of the claims is on the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities, or instead on a process that qualifies as an 'abstract idea' for which computers are invoked merely as a tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to decide whether the claim is directed to an improvement in existing computer technology (favoring eligibility) or to an abstract idea implemented on conventional computers (likely ineligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Look to specification to identify improvements and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the determination of whether these claims are directed to an improvement in existing computer technology, the court looked to the teachings of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specification teachings that show advantages over conventional systems (e.g., increased flexibility, faster search times, smaller memory requirements). The improvement need not be physical; logical structures and processes can define a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement need not be defined by physical components
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvement does not need to be defined by reference to 'physical' components. Instead, the improvement here is defined by logical structures and processes, rather than particular physical features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept non-physical (logical/architectural/algorithmic) improvements as potentially demonstrating non-abstract character, provided the claim and specification support that characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim is directed to a computer-technology improvement, Step 2B may be unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may determine that a claim directed to improvements in computer-related technology is not directed to an abstract idea under Step 2A (and is thus patent eligible), without the need to analyze the additional elements under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Step 2A shows the claim is directed to a specific improvement in computer functionality, do not proceed to Step 2B if no abstract-idea finding is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional elements must add 'significantly more' beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activities (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is found to be directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A), the additional elements must add significantly more. Elements that are well-understood, routine, conventional activities do not add significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether elements such as using a telephone unit and a server are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' — if so, they do not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter under Step 2B (as in TLI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely implement abstract processes on conventional computers are likely abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to generalized steps to be performed on a computer using conventional computer activity (e.g., recording, administration and archiving of digital images) can be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claimed steps are general organizational/classification activities implemented using routine computer components, treat them as more likely to be abstract absent a specific improvement in computer technology.
